extracted.intended_audience: readers and critics of literary fiction; authors (particularly novelists) interested in critical standards
extracted.subtask_description: Literary-critical guidance and evaluative criteria for judging (and for women producing) novels and poetic historical re-creations, with attention to subject-matter, style, characterization, moral seriousness, and historical fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate choice of social milieu for Evangelical fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Evangelical novelists should seek their subjects among the middle and lower classes rather than gratuitously among titles and carriages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that 'the real drama of Evangelicalism... lies among the middle and lower classes' and asks why Evangelical lady novelists cannot 'show us the operation of their religious views among people... who keep no carriage.' Selecting aristocratic settings for Evangelical fiction is criticized as both inauthentic and ill-judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating conversion as merely fashionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not depict religious conversion as a superficial change of social décor (same tastes, different guests); conversion should be shown in genuine effects on life and character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic condemns novels where a worldly woman is merely 'converted' but retains the same fondness for fine dining and dress—only now she 'invites clergymen instead of beaux' and trivial conversation is 'flavored with gospel instead of gossip.' Such travesties are labeled nauseating and unconvincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful and specific representation of manners and conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Depictions of fashionable society or particular social types must be convincing and precise rather than curious or superficial studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Evangelical novelists sometimes produce 'curious studies' of fashionable society, the essay praises 'meritoriously realistic' pictures where the author really understands the manners and conversations she seeks to represent; vague or second-hand portrayals are censured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid insipid, stereotyped heroes (the Evangelical young curate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on the stock, insipid Evangelical young curate as a hero; characterization must go beyond the ordinary type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay notes that the favorite Evangelical hero is 'always rather an insipid personage' and implies authors should avoid this easy stereotype and aim for more vigorous, individualized characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue and narrative must represent something intelligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue should not be drivelling or merely ornamented with italics and innuendo; narrative must indicate and represent clearly what it intends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sample of 'drivelling' dialogue (with 'profuse italics and palpable innuendoes') is given as an example of bad practice: such talk 'represents nothing, and barely indicates what is meant to be represented.' Avoid vague, over-stylized speech and narratorial emptiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vulgarisms of style that betray limited social knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Questionable English and vulgarisms in style reveal inadequate experience of the social worlds the author attempts to depict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic points out that certain vulgarisms 'sufficiently indicate' the author's social milieu and that such lapses show she 'has had the advantage, though she has been unable to use it, of mingling chiefly with men and women whose manners... have not had all their bosses and angles rubbed down by refined conventionalism.' Style should fit subject and social knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/modern-antique fiction requires rare exact knowledge and genius
rubrics_metrics.description: To reanimate the past convincingly an author needs both accurate, minute historical knowledge and creative sympathetic divination; this combination is very rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay states that the 'finest effort to reanimate the past... demands as much accurate and minute knowledge as creative vigor' and that modern-antique novels often expose mediocrity when authors clothe feeble sentimentality in ancient names without genuine understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not transpose modern sentiment into ancient characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid putting 'feeble sentimentality' or modern rhetorical arguments into the mouths of historical or mythic personages—it's a masquerade that reveals mediocrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors who attribute modern sentiment or rhetorical modes to 'Roman vestals or Egyptian princesses' or to 'Jewish high-priests and Greek philosophers' are criticized for making their mediocrity conspicuous by taking on an unjustifiable task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of language: prefer plainness over grandiloquence when inappropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain language is often better than an affected antique grandiloquence; ornamental grand style used to fake 'antique coloring' is condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay ridicules the 'peculiar style of grandiloquence which is held by some lady novelists to give an antique coloring' and contrasts that with the value of clear, plain language; examples of affected phrases are cited as proofs of the vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral qualities required for literary excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary excellence demands patient diligence, a sense of responsibility in publication, and an appreciation of the sacredness of the writer's art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic argues that deficiencies in feminine literature are due less to want of intellect than to lack of these moral qualities. The absence of self-criticism and sense of responsibility yields facility and imbecile combination; cultivating these moral habits would check futile authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-criticism and high standards to prevent facile facility
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must apply self-criticism to avoid mistaking easily produced writing for mastery; without high standards, fertility becomes imbecile combination or feeble imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay compares literary facility without standard to singing without an ear: 'a degree more melodic sensibility would suffice to render them silent.' Encourages authors to check their impulses to publish and to cultivate restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation: avoid writing from vanity; value necessity and labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing from vanity leads to 'busy idleness' and trash; those who write from necessity (for livelihood) are less likely to produce the worst literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'standing apology' that society shuts women from other occupations is acknowledged, but the author suggests that three women write from vanity for every one who writes from necessity. The productive vice of vanity should be guarded against.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right elements of fiction: genuine observation, humor, and passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction's 'right elements' are genuine observation, humor, and passion—pour in the right elements and the novel may take any beautiful form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay asserts that fiction is flexible in form but requires these core ingredients; they are what make novels 'fine' and distinctive, and are accessible to women as to men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the seductive lack of external technical barriers in novel-writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Because novel-writing lacks rigid technical requirements, it can seduce incompetent writers into mistaking facility for mastery—authors must supply internal discipline instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic notes that other arts have techniques that guard against intrusion of incapacity, but the novel has 'no barriers for incapacity to stumble against.' Therefore self-restraint and internal standards are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic sincerity: avoid sycophancy and bombast driven by patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry that flatters patrons or rhapsodizes in a manner motivated by patronage (sycophant-praise) or produces 'furious bombast' is morally and artistically suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In discussing Edward Young, the essay criticizes verses of fulsome dedication and extravagant laudation (to patrons and monarchs) as signs of a poet whose genius is compromised by worldly ambition and obsequiousness.
